name: Gelatine
note: Made by boiling animal bones, skin and connective tissue, usually from pigs or cattle. Found in jellies, marshmallows, gummy sweets, some yoghurts and wine gums. Not vegan.

name: Rennet (animal)
note: An enzyme traditionally taken from the stomach lining of young calves, used to set cheese. UK labels don't always say which kind is used, so 'rennet' alone on a cheese is worth treating as animal unless it's marked vegetarian, microbial or 'suitable for vegetarians'. Not vegan.

name: Vegetarian or microbial rennet
note: A lab-grown or fungal alternative to animal rennet, used to set cheese without slaughtering an animal. It doesn't involve an animal directly, though I'd still check with the specific cheese brand if you want full certainty either way.

name: Whey
note: A liquid by-product of cheesemaking from cow's milk, usually dried into a powder. Turns up in crisps, biscuits, protein bars and bread well beyond the dairy aisle. Not vegan.

name: Casein
note: A milk protein used as a thickener, including in some products labelled 'dairy-free' - it's not a dairy sugar, so it can slip past a lactose-free claim. Not vegan.

name: Lactose
note: The natural sugar found in milk, used as a bulking agent in some medicines and processed foods. Not vegan.

name: Honey
note: Made by honeybees from nectar, used as a sweetener in food, drinks and baking. Not vegan.
detail: Honey is made by bees, for bees, as their food store, and commercial beekeeping is set up to maximise how much of it gets taken for us instead. Beekeepers often clip a queen's wings to stop her leaving to start a new colony elsewhere, since that would cut into the hive's output. When honey is harvested, it's commonly replaced with a cheap sugar syrup that lacks the nutrients real honey gave the colony, which can leave bees malnourished over winter. Hives are also selectively bred for higher yield, which narrows the gene pool and makes colonies more vulnerable to disease and mass die-offs, and underperforming hives can be culled outright to cut costs. None of this needs bees to be treated badly on purpose, it's just what happens when an animal's own food supply becomes a commercial product.

name: Beeswax (E901)
note: Made by honeybees, sometimes used as a glazing agent on sweets, fruit and cheese rinds for shine or a protective coating. Not vegan.
detail: Beeswax comes from the same commercial hives as honey, so it carries the same underlying issues: selectively bred colonies, queens with clipped wings, and hives culled if they're not productive enough. Bees also have to work harder to rebuild the wax comb that's taken from them, on top of losing their own food store. It's easy to think of beeswax as a harmless leftover, but it's produced by the same industry, under the same conditions, as honey.

name: Cochineal / carmine (E120)
note: A red colouring made by crushing cochineal insects, used in some sweets, drinks, yoghurts and processed meats. Not vegan.

name: Isinglass
note: Made from fish swim bladders, traditionally used to clarify some beers and wines. It's usually removed before bottling, but as a processing aid rather than a listed ingredient it often won't appear on the label at all - the only reliable way to know is a vegan-certified logo or asking the brewery directly. Not vegan.

name: Lard
note: Rendered pig fat, used in some pastry, bread and baked goods for texture. Not vegan.

name: Tallow / suet
note: Rendered fat from cattle or sheep. Suet is traditionally used in puddings, mincemeat and some pastry; tallow is sometimes used for frying, including by some fast food chains. Not vegan.

name: Shellac (E904)
note: A resin secreted by the lac bug, used to give shine to sweets, chocolate coatings and sometimes fresh fruit like apples. Also sold as 'confectioner's glaze'. Not vegan.

name: L-cysteine (E920)
note: A dough conditioner used in some bread and baked goods. It can be synthetic, plant-derived, or made from duck feathers or human hair, and the source usually isn't stated on the label.

name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
note: Often added to fortified cereals, plant milks and margarine. Traditionally made from lanolin (sheep's wool grease), but increasingly made from lichen and sold as vegan D3 - check the label rather than assuming. Vitamin D2 is always plant-derived.

name: Anchovies
note: Small fish, often used as a flavour base rather than an obvious ingredient - easy to miss in Worcestershire sauce, Caesar dressing and some savoury seasonings. Not vegan.

name: Fish oil / marine omega-3
note: Fish-derived oil added to some foods and supplements for omega-3. Plant alternatives (algae oil, flaxseed, chia) exist, but 'omega-3' alone doesn't tell you the source. Not vegan.

name: Glycerin / glycerol (E422)
note: Used as a sweetener or carrier in food and drinks. Can come from animal fat, plant oils, or be made synthetically - look for 'vegetable glycerin' if you want certainty.

name: Natural flavourings
note: A legal term that can cover flavour compounds from plants, animals or fungi, and labelling isn't required to say which. Shows up often in crisps and processed snacks - I only treat it as vegan when a brand confirms it or the product carries a vegan certification.

name: Mono- and diglycerides (E471)
note: A common emulsifier in bread, margarine and ice cream. Can be made from animal fat or plant oils, and the label doesn't have to say which - often plant-derived commercially, but not guaranteed.

name: Egg / albumin
note: Used widely in baking, pasta, mayonnaise and some wine and beer fining. Albumin/albumen usually means egg white specifically. Not vegan.
